content: Jatropha incentives in India are part of the country's strategic plan to achieve energy independence by 2012. Jatropha oil, derived from the seeds of the Jatropha curcas plant, is recognized as an excellent source of bio-diesel. This plant thrives in wastelands across India, making it a sustainable option for energy production. India is actively working to reduce its reliance on coal and petroleum to meet its growing energy demands, and the promotion of Jatropha cultivation is a key element of this energy policy. Large tracts of wasteland have been earmarked for Jatropha cultivation, which is expected to provide significant employment opportunities for the rural poor. Businesses are also viewing Jatropha cultivation as a lucrative opportunity. The Indian government has identified 400,000 square kilometers of land suitable for Jatropha cultivation, with the aim of replacing 20% of the country's diesel consumption by 2011. Former President of India, Dr. Abdul Kalam, has been a strong advocate for Jatropha cultivation to produce bio-diesel. In a recent speech, he highlighted that out of the 60 million hectares of wasteland available in India, over 30 million hectares are suitable for Jatropha cultivation. Once planted, Jatropha has a productive lifespan of several decades and requires minimal water compared to other cash crops. The government has allocated 3 billion rupees to support local farmers in cultivating Jatropha. Farmers can repay loans using the income generated from selling Jatropha seeds to companies like D1 Mohan. The Indian Railways has successfully started using Jatropha oil blended with diesel fuel to power its diesel engines. Currently, diesel locomotives operating on routes such as Thanjavur to Nagore and Tiruchirappalli to Lalgudi, Dindigul, and Karur are running on a blend of Jatropha and diesel oil. In Andhra Pradesh, the state has entered into a formal agreement with Reliance Industries for Jatropha cultivation. The company has selected 200 acres of land in Kakinada to grow Jatropha for high-quality bio-diesel production. Kerala is also planning a large-scale Jatropha planting campaign. Chhattisgarh has committed to planting 160 million Jatropha saplings across its 16 districts in 2006, aiming to become a bio-fuel self-reliant state by 2015. The state expects to generate 40 billion rupees annually from seed sales after 2010. In 2005, Chief Minister Raman Singh became the first state leader to use Jatropha diesel for his official vehicle. Chhattisgarh plans to transition all state-owned diesel and petrol vehicles to Jatropha fuel by 2007. The Chhattisgarh Biofuel Development Authority oversees the production of Jatropha curcas seeds as a rich source of bio-diesel. In Karnataka, farmers in semi-arid regions are planting Jatropha due to its suitability for such conditions. K. Nagendrappa, initially indifferent to Jatropha, now plans to cultivate 12 acres of the plant on his land near Bangalore. Tamil Nadu is aggressively promoting Jatropha cultivation to help farmers recover from losses caused by irregular rainfall in recent years. The government has contracted large-scale Jatropha development to four companies: M/s Mohan Breweries and Distilleries Limited, M/s Shiva Distilleries Limited, M/s Dharani Sugars and Chemicals Limited, and M/s Riverway Agro Products Private Ltd. These firms have cultivated Jatropha on approximately 3 square kilometers, with a target of 50 square kilometers. The Tamil Nadu government has also abolished purchase tax on Jatropha. Rajasthan is an ideal location for Jatropha cultivation due to its minimal water requirements, which is crucial in this water-scarce region. Jatropha plantations have been established in districts such as Udaipur, Kota, Sikar, Banswara, Chittor, and Churu. In Udaipur, Jatropha is planted in agroforestry formats alongside food or cash crops on marginal lands. Its toxic leaves make it unpalatable to livestock, ensuring the saplings remain intact. In Maharashtra, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) has partnered with the Maharashtra State Farming Corporation Ltd (MSFCL) for a Jatropha seed-based bio-diesel venture. Jatropha is being cultivated on 500 acres in Nashik and Aurangabad. In 2005, the Maharashtra government aimed to cultivate Jatropha on 600 square kilometers, with half the land allocated to the public sector and the other half to the private sector. Pune Municipal Corporation became the first Indian city to use Jatropha-based bio-diesel in over 100 public buses in July 2006. In Ahmednagar, Gulabrao Kale studied the potential of Jatropha plantations and, under his guidance, the Govind Gramin Vikas Pratishthan (GOGVIP) initiated a plantation program under the government's DPAP scheme. Initially, convincing farmers to adopt Jatropha cultivation was challenging due to low literacy levels and skepticism about its future benefits. However, after persistent efforts, over 1,000 farmers are now participating in the program. GOGVIP has planted more than 2 million Jatropha plants across five villages: Vankute, Dhoki, Dhotre, Dhavalpuri, and Gajdipoor. These remote villages posed connectivity challenges, but the program has successfully established Jatropha plantations in the area.
